info.title: Go-Ticket-System API
info.description:
A help desk ticket system: tickets in queues, the customers they come from and what is written in them.

Authenticate either with the session cookie obtained from `POST /auth/login`, or with a personal API token sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-API-Token: <token>`.

A token carries no rights of its own: every request is evaluated against the owner's **current** role, so changing or revoking a role takes effect on the very next call.

All responses are wrapped by the framework as `{"data": ...}` on success and `{"error": {"message": ...}}` on failure.

tags.name: settings
tags.description: Instance administration, for whoever administers the installation

tags.name: tickets
tags.description: What tickets are sorted by - the states, the priorities and the types - and, as the ticket system grows, the tickets themselves.

tags.name: customers
tags.description: Who tickets come from: the organisations and their contacts. Reading takes `customers:read` and changing `customers:write`, and neither is narrowed by queue.

tags.name: automation
tags.description: What the application does to tickets by itself: the macros, run as the application on every ticket they are given. Takes `automation:write`.

tags.name: portal
tags.description: The customer's side: the tickets of the contact the account signs in as - their own, and their organisation's where the contact sees them - whatever queue they are in, and only what a customer is shown of them. Takes `portal:use`; a ticket the caller does not follow is not found.

tags.name: catalog
tags.description: The general catalog, as KIX18 keeps it: the lists the configuration items and the changes pick from. Read by every account signed in; changed with `catalog:write`. Nothing is deleted from it - a value no longer offered is retired.

tags.name: assets
tags.description: The configuration items, as KIX18 keeps its assets: an item of a class, in versions each written under the definition its class had then. Read with `assets:read`, written with `assets:write`; a version is never changed, a change to an item is its next version.

totp.description: Required when the account has two-factor authentication enabled.

201.description: Signed in; a session cookie is set. When the response says `totpRequired`, no cookie is set and the code must be supplied.

get.summary: Whether passkeys can be used on this connection
get.description: Browsers expose WebAuthn only on a secure context - HTTPS, or localhost - and reject an IP address as a relying party identifier. The interface asks before offering a button that could only fail with "SecurityError: This is an invalid domain".

post.description: Returns a challenge. No username is asked for: the browser offers whichever credentials it holds for this site, and the one that signs names its own owner.

put.description: Verifies the signature and opens a session, exactly as a password sign-in does - same cookie, same lifetime, same CSRF rotation. Every failure answers alike.

get.summary: Whether a Kerberos sign-in is on offer
get.description: True where a keytab was read at start and a directory is configured to look a ticket's owner up in. The interface asks before trying one, so a browser on an installation without either is never sent the Negotiate challenge.

post.summary: Sign in with a Kerberos ticket
post.description: The ticket travels as `Authorization: Negotiate …`, which a browser sends by itself once it trusts this address; a request without one is answered 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate`, the challenge that asks for it. Only a ticket of the keytab's realm is accepted. Its owner is looked up in the directory - as named, then as name@REALM - and signed in to the account a directory password sign-in reaches, with the same session, cookie and CSRF rotation. A second factor the account holds is asked for with `totpRequired`, and the code is sent back as `totp` with the ticket.

totp.description: Required when the account has two-factor authentication enabled.

201.description: Signed in; a session cookie is set. When the response says `totpRequired`, no cookie is set and the code must be supplied.

401.description: No ticket, a ticket that does not verify, or an owner the directory does not hold. Without a ticket the answer carries `WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate`.

409.description: No keytab was read at start (`kerberosOff`), or no directory is configured to look a ticket's owner up in (`kerberosNeedsDirectory`).

get.summary: Whether signing in through a provider is offered
get.description: Answers {"offered": true, "label": "Keycloak"} when a provider is configured and switched on under Settings, {"offered": false} otherwise. Reachable without a session: the sign-in form asks it before there is anybody to ask for.

post.summary: Start signing in through the provider
post.description: No body. Answers {"address": "https://..."}, the provider's own sign-in to send the browser to, and sets a cookie holding the round's state, so that only this browser can finish it. The provider sends the browser back to /sign-in/openid, which is a page of the interface rather than a route of this API: the page hands the code and the state it came back with to POST /auth/openid/finish. openidOff when no provider is configured, openidUnreachable when its discovery document cannot be read.

post.summary: Finish a round through the provider
post.description: Body: {"state": "...", "code": "..."}, as the browser came back with them. Only the browser holding the round's cookie can finish it, once, within ten minutes, and with the provider that was configured when it began (attemptExpired otherwise). The code is traded with the PKCE verifier the round was begun with, and the identity token is believed only when it is signed with the provider's published key, for this installation's client, not expired and carrying the round's nonce (openidRefused otherwise). A round begun by POST /me/openid links the account whose session began it and answers in the shape GET /me/openid does; any other signs in the account the identity is linked to and answers as POST /auth/login does, setting the session cookie. An identity nobody linked opens nothing (openidNotLinked): no account is ever matched on an address or made for an identity. The built-in administrator and an account the directory holds are never signed in this way (adminHasNoOpenID, directoryAccountHasNoOpenID).

201.description: Signed in, or the account linked

400.description: attemptExpired

409.description: The provider refused, or the identity opens no account here

post.summary: Sign out and end the session
Sign in to the web interface with a personal token
post.description: The token travels as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` or `X-API-Token`, and the answer is a sign-in's: the session cookie, a new CSRF cookie and `{"user": {...}, "permissions": [...]}`. It is how the Android app signs in to the web interface it shows, connected by the code a new token is shown with. It grants nothing the token does not - the token already carries its owner's role through the API - and only the token decides who: a session cookie on the same request is not asked. The session ends with the token: revoking the token ends it, and it lasts no longer than the token does. A token that does not resolve is answered 401 as a wrong password is, one whose owner is still on the initial password 409 mustChangePasswordFirst, and during maintenance only an account that may end it gets a session.

201.description: Signed in; a session cookie is set

401.description: The token is not one this installation knows

409.description: The token's owner has to change the initial password first

get.summary: The signed-in user and their permissions
get.description: Answers {"user", "permissions", "authEnabled", "permissionsRevision"}. permissionsRevision changes exactly when what the account may do changes; every response carries the current one in the X-Permissions-Revision header, and this is the baseline to compare it against.

put.summary: Change your own password; ends every session you have

400.description: Wrong current password, or the new one is too short
Unsupported language

put.summary: Set the appearance you read in, or clear it to follow the time of day
put.description: "light", "dark", or an empty value. Empty is meaningful rather than an omission: it is how somebody goes back to the screen following the time of day. The appearance is stored on the account rather than in the browser, so a shared machine does not hand the next person the last one's.

400.description: Unknown appearance

put.summary: Set your own timezone, or clear it to follow the instance
put.description: An IANA name such as "Europe/Berlin". An empty value is meaningful: it clears the personal setting so the account follows the instance-wide zone again. An unknown name is rejected rather than stored, because it would otherwise fall back to UTC at every use and write every moment in a zone nobody chose.

put.summary: Record whether you have been shown the guided tour
put.description: Stored on the user rather than in the browser, so someone who has been introduced to the application is not introduced again on their next device. Settable both ways: sending false offers the tour again, which is how the "Show the tour" button works.

get.description: Carries no key material. The public half could be sent harmlessly - it verifies signatures and cannot produce them - but sending it invites building something on a value that is meaningless outside a ceremony. `createdAt` and `lastUsedAt` are RFC 3339 moments rather than dates, for the reason the token listing gives.

post.description: Refused for the built-in administrator: it is the guaranteed way back into an installation, and a guarantee that depends on a particular device still existing is not one.

put.description: Verifies what the authenticator created and stores the public half.

delete.description: Scoped to the owner, so an id from somewhere else deletes nothing. Allowed even for the last one: a passkey is an addition to the password, never a replacement, so removing it cannot lock anyone out.

post.summary: Begin two-factor enrolment; the secret is returned once

put.summary: Confirm two-factor with a current code

400.description: Invalid code
Invalid code

get.summary: List your API tokens; secrets are never returned
get.description: `createdAt`, `expiresAt` and `lastUsedAt` are RFC 3339 moments, not dates. They used to be days, which is the wrong answer for the field somebody reads when they think a token has been taken: a token used at three in the morning read exactly like one used at three in the afternoon, and one used twice today read as used once. A use is written down at most once a minute, so `lastUsedAt` can be up to a minute behind the latest one.

post.summary: Issue an API token; the secret is shown once and cannot be recovered

expiresInDays.description: 0 means the token does not expire on its own.

201.description: The token, including its `secret`, and what an app connects with: `connectUri`, which is `go-ticket-system://connect?token=<the secret>&url=<this installation>` - the address being the one the request reached the installation at - and `qr`, that address as a QR code in an SVG data URI. All three exist only in this response.

409.description: Token limit reached

delete.summary: Revoke one of your own tokens
delete.description: The sessions the token was exchanged for through `POST /auth/token` end with it.

409.description: Email already in use

get.summary: Read a user; your own account needs no permission

409.description: The built-in administrator must keep a role that can administer, an account from the directory keeps its name and address, and an account a contact signs in to the portal with is given no role that administers
The account owns unfinished tickets and nothing was confirmed, or it is one that cannot be deleted

delete.description: An account that owns tickets which are not finished is refused with deletionNeedsConfirming and their number; ?confirm=true says that whoever asked knows those tickets are left without an owner. The tickets stay either way, and what the account wrote in them stays without its name. The built-in administrator (adminUndeletable), the caller's own account (cannotDeleteSelf) and an account the directory holds (directoryAccountUndeletable) are refused whatever is confirmed. Needs `users:delete`.

parameters.name: confirm
parameters.description: true to delete an account that owns unfinished tickets, which are left without an owner

409.description: The built-in administrator must keep a role that can administer, and an account a contact signs in to the portal with is given none that does

put.description: Gives an account a password chosen by whoever holds users:write, for letting somebody back in who has forgotten theirs. The account is flagged to replace it before it can use anything, and every session it has open ends. Refused for the caller’s own account, which is changed through /me/password with the current password, and for a directory account, whose password lives in the directory.

400.description: The password is too short

409.description: Your own account, or one kept in the directory

delete.description: For somebody who has lost the phone their second factor was on: turns off the code from the authenticator app, deletes every passkey the account holds and ends every session it has open, so its password alone signs it in again. Needs users:write. Refused for the caller’s own account, whose second factor is turned off under /me/totp with a code from it, and for an account that has no second factor to remove. Recorded in the administration log.

409.description: Your own account, or one with no second factor

400.description: Unknown permission

post.description: A role has to grant at least one permission: one that grants nothing can be assigned, and whoever holds it signs in to an interface with nothing on it.

409.description: System roles cannot be renamed or weakened, and a role accounts of contacts hold is given no right that administers

put.description: A system role may be described differently and nothing else: not renamed, and its permissions not changed in either direction. It is the role the built-in administrator holds, and an installation that could weaken it could lock itself out of its own administration.

409.description: System role, or the role is still assigned

get.summary: What the installation adds to its name, its logo and footer
get.description: Public on purpose: the sign-in screen needs it before anyone is authenticated. Every installation is called Go-Ticket-System; title is what follows it after a bar (Go-Ticket-System | title), and tabTitle what follows it in the browser tab, the title's where tabTitle is empty. Empty adds nothing.

get.summary: What a fresh installation still has to settle
get.description: Each step reports whether it is done, worked out from what is actually configured rather than from a record of the wizard having been shown - so a setting that is undone makes its step outstanding again. Two steps are required (the administrator password and the timezone); the rest are optional. Built-in administrator only, because a list of what is not yet configured is a useful thing for an attacker to read. Deliberately reachable while the initial password blocks the rest of the API.

post.description: Records that the wizard was dismissed, which settles the optional steps only. It reappears by itself while any required step is outstanding, so this cannot be used to run an installation without a timezone.

post.summary: Claim the session the installer earned
post.description: Answered before anybody is signed in, and only on a process that actually served an installer. The browser holding that installer’s setup token is given a session for the built-in administrator, so the first screen after the installation is the one asking for a password rather than one asking for the documented initial password. Refused once a password has been chosen, and refused entirely on an installation configured without the installer.

parameters.name: X-Setup-Token
parameters.description: The token the installer printed to this process’s log.

409.description: No installer ran, or the installation has already been taken into use

get.description: Returns three things: the values an administrator has overridden, the values currently in force, and the values the configuration file supplies. An absent field under "configured" means that limit still follows the file.

put.description: Send only the fields to override; omitting one makes it follow the configuration file again, and an empty object resets everything. Values are bounded on save, because this screen can otherwise lock out its own administrator. Takes effect within seconds, without a restart. Administrator only.

get.description: Answers {"place": "DE-BY", "countries": [{"code": "DE", "regions": ["BW", "BY"], "regionRequired": true}]}: the place whose public holidays the installation's service hours leave out - a country by its ISO 3166-1 code, with its region after a dash where it has one - "none" where the installation chose to keep none, or empty while nobody has chosen; both of those keep none. countries is every place a choice can name, and whether a region has to be named with it. For whoever administers the installation.

put.description: Body: {"place": "DE-BY"} - a place as GET names them, "none", or empty. A country the rules do not know is refused naming the field country, and a region its country does not have - or a country that needs one, without - naming the field region.
The zone a ticket's number takes its day from and the service hours are read in, and the one a moment is written in for every account that has not set its own. Administrator only.

get.summary: Read the stored database connection; the password is never returned

put.summary: Save the database connection; applied on the next restart
put.description: An empty password keeps the one in force, and only for the same type, host, port and user: a connection naming another server or user is sent no password it was not given.

get.summary: Read the logging, metrics and tracing settings
get.description: Returns what has been administered under "configured" and what this process is actually writing, serving and exporting under "active". The two disagree until the next restart. An absent field under "configured" follows the configuration file; "traceExporter": "" is an administered off, which is a different thing. Administrator only.

put.summary: Set the logging, metrics and tracing settings; applied on the next restart
put.description: Send only the fields to administer; an empty object makes everything follow the configuration file again. "logLevel" is DEBUG, INFO, NOTICE, WARN, ERROR or FATAL. "traceExporter" is "otlp", "jaeger" or "" for off, and needs "tracerUrl" as host:port when it names an exporter, with https:// in front to encrypt the export or http:// or nothing for plaintext - another scheme or a path is refused, because the exporter speaks OTLP over gRPC. "metricsOff": true stops the metrics endpoint being served; the port itself stays in the configuration file, because GoFr refuses to start when something already holds it. The log level takes effect on the next line written; the rest is applied when the application is restarted, because GoFr binds the port and builds the exporter while starting up. Administrator only.

post.summary: Probe a database connection without saving or switching to it
post.description: An empty password keeps the one in force, and only for the same type, host, port and user: a connection naming another server or user is sent no password it was not given.

201.description: Result; the `ok` field tells success from failure

get.summary: Read the LDAP configuration; the bind password is never returned

put.summary: Save the LDAP configuration; takes effect immediately

get.summary: The provider people sign in through
get.description: Answers {"enabled", "issuer", "clientId", "label", "hasSecret", "redirectUri"}. The client secret is never sent back; hasSecret says whether one is stored. redirectUri is the address to register at the provider: this installation as the browser asking reached it, followed by /sign-in/openid.

put.summary: Configure the provider people sign in through
put.description: Body: {"enabled", "issuer", "clientId", "clientSecret", "label"}. An empty clientSecret keeps the stored one. The issuer is the provider's address exactly as its tokens name it - Keycloak's realm address, an Entra ID tenant's v2.0 address, https://accounts.google.com - and has to be reached over HTTPS unless it is on this machine (openidNeedsHttps). The secret is sealed with SECRET_KEY where it is stored. Applies from the next sign-in.

200.description: The stored provider, as GET answers

post.summary: Read a provider's discovery document without saving anything
post.description: Body: {"issuer": "..."}. Answers {"ok": true}, or {"ok": false, "error": {"code", "message", "detail"}} with what the provider said in detail.

201.description: Result; the `ok` field tells success from failure

post.summary: Probe an LDAP connection without saving it

201.description: Result; the `ok` field tells success from failure

get.summary: Your link to an identity at the provider
get.description: Answers {"linked": true, "issuer": "https://id.example.com", "linkedAt": "2026-10-20T09:30:00Z"}, or {"linked": false}.

post.summary: Start linking your account to your identity at the provider
post.description: No body. Answers as POST /auth/openid does; the round, finished by the same browser in the same session, links this account to whoever signs in at the provider. From then on that identity signs this account in without its password and without its second factor - the provider asks its own. Refused for the built-in administrator and for an account the directory holds, and for an identity already linked to another account (openidLinkedElsewhere).

delete.summary: Unlink your account from the provider
delete.description: The provider signs this account in no more. 404 when it is linked to nothing.

get.summary: Everything held about your own account, as a ZIP
get.description: Answers application/zip: a JSON file per part - account, owned-tickets, tickets-responsible-for, contact, watched-tickets, notifications, queues-told-about, api-tokens, passkeys, sessions, push-subscriptions, openid-links, written-articles - each an array of rows with the columns as they are stored, and about.json saying what the archive is and what it leaves out. It holds what erasing the account would delete or take the account's name off, and where and when the account wrote in tickets - not what it wrote, because an answer quotes the customer it answers. Left out as well are the password's hash, the second factor's seed, the hashes of personal tokens and sessions, and a passkey's key material: what is handed over about those is that they exist, when they were made and when they were last used. Open to anybody signed in, the built-in administrator included, and only ever about their own account (GDPR articles 15 and 20). Without authentication there is no account to export (noAuthNoAccount).

get.summary: Whether the caller's browsers can be pushed to
get.description: Answers {"enabled": true, "publicKey": "BP4z...", "endpoints": ["https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/..."]}: whether the installation pushes notifications, the key a browser subscribes with - empty while it does not - and the addresses of the caller's own subscribed browsers, so a page can tell whether the one it is open in is among them. Needs `tickets:read`.

post.summary: Push the caller's notifications to a browser
post.description: Takes the browser's subscription as the browser writes it out, {"endpoint": "...", "keys": {"p256dh": "...", "auth": "..."}}, and answers as GET does. Refused with pushOff while the installation does not push, pushServiceUnknown for an address that is not the push service of a browser's maker over https, and pushSubscriptionInvalid for keys no message can be encrypted for. A browser subscribed by another account before is this caller's from then on. Needs `tickets:read`.

200.description: The caller's push state, with this browser among the endpoints

400.description: Not a push service, or not a push channel's keys

409.description: The installation does not push notifications

delete.summary: Stop pushing to one of the caller's browsers
delete.description: Takes {"endpoint": "..."}, and forgets that browser if it is one of the caller's. Signed in is all it needs, so that no right withdrawn since keeps somebody from taking a browser of theirs back.

200.description: The browser is not pushed to

get.summary: This installation's address, and the same as a QR code
get.description: Answers {"address": "https://tickets.example.com", "qr": "data:image/svg+xml;base64,..."}. `?origin=` names the address the asking page is at, its location.origin, and is taken where it names the host the request reached, with http or https; otherwise the address is this installation as the request reached it. The code is for opening the installation on a phone without typing its address. Needs nothing beyond being signed in.

get.summary: Where the Android app of this installation is downloaded, and the same as a QR code
get.description: Answers {"release": "https://github.com/dennis-dko/go-ticket-system/releases/tag/v0.4.8", "download": "https://github.com/dennis-dko/go-ticket-system/releases/download/v0.4.8/go-ticket-system-mobile_v0.4.8.apk", "version": "v0.4.8", "qr": "data:image/svg+xml;base64,..."}. The app belongs to the release it was built with, so these are the release this installation runs; an installation that runs no release - a build from source - is given the newest release's page and neither a download nor a version. version is what the Android app compares its own with at every start, offering to download and install the app at download where it is newer. The code is of the download, or of the page where there is none, for a phone's camera. Needs nothing beyond being signed in.
Needs `users:read`. No password is included, in either direction.

parameters.name: lang
parameters.description: Language for the column headings and the values inside them, e.g. `de`. Unknown or absent means English. The importer reads a file in any of these languages whatever this was set to, because the heading row is skipped by position and translated values are recognised in every language.

post.description: Changes existing accounts, matched on the email address, and does not create them: a new account needs a password, and a password in a spreadsheet is a password that gets mailed around. An empty cell leaves that setting as it is. Needs `users:write`. Every row is reported either way: the ones that would be written and the ones that cannot, with the reason. Nothing is written while any row is refused - a file half imported leaves somebody looking for which half.

parameters.name: lang
parameters.description: Language for the column headings and the values inside them, e.g. `de`. Unknown or absent means English. The importer reads a file in any of these languages whatever this was set to, because the heading row is skipped by position and translated values are recognised in every language.

dryRun.description: `true` previews without writing anything. Send the file twice - once to look, once to write - rather than relying on a plan held between requests.

200.description: What the file would do, or what it did

201.description: What the file would do, or what it did

400.description: Not a readable workbook of this kind

409.description: Some rows cannot be written, so nothing was

get.summary: Export roles as .xlsx, a column per permission
get.description: Needs `roles:read`. Every permission the application enforces gets a column holding yes or no, rather than one cell listing them: a typo in a list is a right silently dropped, and nothing about it looks wrong until somebody cannot open a screen. The permission columns are not translated - a permission is an identifier, and the role editor shows it verbatim.

parameters.name: lang
parameters.description: Language for the column headings and the values inside them, e.g. `de`. Unknown or absent means English. The importer reads a file in any of these languages whatever this was set to, because the heading row is skipped by position and translated values are recognised in every language.

post.description: Creates and changes roles, matched on the name. Needs `roles:write`. A permission column is read by its heading rather than by position, so a file exported before a right existed still imports correctly; a heading naming a permission this application does not enforce is refused, because it means the file came from somewhere else. A system role may be described differently and nothing else - its permissions are what keeps the installation administrable. Every row is reported either way, and nothing is written while any row is refused.

parameters.name: lang
parameters.description: Language for the column headings and the values inside them, e.g. `de`. Unknown or absent means English. The importer reads a file in any of these languages whatever this was set to, because the heading row is skipped by position and translated values are recognised in every language.

dryRun.description: `true` previews without writing anything. Send the file twice - once to look, once to write - rather than relying on a plan held between requests.

200.description: What the file would do, or what it did

201.description: What the file would do, or what it did

400.description: Not a readable workbook of this kind, or a permission column naming a right this application does not enforce - that one answers `unknownPermissionColumn` with the offending heading, since the file itself reads perfectly well

409.description: Some rows cannot be written, so nothing was

get.summary: Whether the installation is in maintenance mode
get.description: Public, like the branding and for the same reason: somebody opening the page during maintenance should read the notice on the sign-in screen rather than watch requests fail silently.

200.description: The maintenance state and its notice

put.summary: Turn maintenance mode on or off
put.description: While it is on, everything but signing in and the settings themselves is refused, so an administrator cannot lock themselves out of turning it off again.

200.description: The state as it now stands

get.summary: What is waiting for a restart
get.description: Lists the stored settings the running process does not match yet. `startedAt` changes when the process does, which is how a client can tell a restart it asked for actually happened.

200.description: Pending changes and the start time

post.description: Only where the platform can do it: the process replaces itself, which needs exec, so it is refused on Windows with a reason naming what to do instead. And only into a database that answers: the connection the next start opens - the stored one, or the environment's where none is stored - is probed first, the way the start probes it, because a start ends on one that does not answer and nothing would be left to put it right from. The refusal carries what the driver said as `detail`.

400.description: The platform cannot restart in place (`restartUnsupported`)

409.description: The database the next start would open does not answer (`restartWouldNotStart`); nothing was restarted

post.summary: What a directory synchronisation would do
post.description: Changes nothing, so an administrator can see which accounts a run would remove, and how many unfinished tickets each of them owns and would leave without an owner, before committing to it.

200.description: The report a run would produce

post.description: Matches on the directory-side identifier rather than the mail address, so a renamed mailbox is not read as a departure. `aborted` carries the reason a guard stopped the run, and `abortCode` with `abortValues` the same reason for a client to put in its reader's language, as with any refusal.

parameters.name: confirmed
parameters.description: The account ids a preview proposed and somebody confirmed, comma-separated; empty for a preview that proposed nobody. Given, the run deletes exactly these or changes nothing (`syncDiffersFromPreview`), because it asks the directory again and the answer may have moved. Absent, the run is unbound and held by the deletion limit alone, as a scheduled run is.

get.summary: List what recent directory runs changed
get.description: The latest runs that removed or added an account, newest first, at most twenty: when each ran, whether somebody confirmed it against a preview (the schedule and a script that sent no list did not), how many accounts it removed, how many tickets those accounts left without an owner, and how many accounts it added. Nothing about whom: the people a run removed are the people the erasure erases, and the log names them for as long as it lasts. For whoever administers the installation, as running one is.

get.summary: Who changed how the installation is run
get.description: Answers {"entries": [{"id", "at", "actor": {"id", "name"}, "action": "user.role", "target": {"id", "name"}, "detail": "agent"}], "more"}, newest first, fifty at a time; ?before= the id of the oldest entry already shown reads the page before it. Every change that went through to an account (user.created, user.updated, user.deleted, user.role, user.password, users.imported), a role (role.created, role.updated, role.deleted, roles.imported), a setting (settings.maintenance with detail true or false, settings.branding, settings.ldap, settings.openid, settings.operational, settings.timezone, settings.holidays, settings.datasource, settings.telemetry) or the installation (directory.synchronised, installation.restart, installation.update, installation.setup) is recorded with the account that made it. Ids are kept and names read now: an account erased since has an empty name, and target is left out for a change to the installation as a whole. Needs settings:manage.
Behind the built-in administrator: the log carries email addresses, request paths and whatever a failing driver decided to print.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Only lines newer than this sequence number.

parameters.name: levels
parameters.description: Comma-separated, e.g. `WARN,ERROR`. Absent means every level.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring of the message. A whole trace - the `traceId` of a record, which is also the `X-Correlation-ID` of the response to that request - finds the lines that request wrote.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many lines at most; the newest are kept.

parameters.name: epoch
parameters.description: The `epoch` of the answer `since` was taken from. Sequence numbers start again with the process, so a position counted by a process that has since been replaced is answered from the beginning of the running one, with `restarted` set.

200.description: Log lines, the levels that exist, how many were dropped or passed over, and the `epoch` to send back with `since`

get.summary: What version is running, and whether a newer one exists
get.description: Answers on every deployment, and says which kind it is. `available` is the only field a button should key on: it means a newer version exists, it published a binary for this platform, this deployment is one where installing lasts, and it has not already been downloaded. `installable` is false in a container - a binary swapped inside one is undone by the next recreate, so the image is what gets updated there. `pending` names a version already on disk and waiting for a restart. A lookup that failed comes back as `problem` with a 200 rather than as an error: the release feed being unreachable is not this application being broken. Needs the rights the built-in administrator has, not merely settings:manage.

200.description: The running version and what is available

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

post.summary: Download and install the newest release
post.description: Downloads the release's binary for this platform, checks it against the SHA256SUMS published beside it, and puts it where this process's own file is. Nothing is written into place until the hash matches - this is code that will be executed as the application on the next start. It does not restart: replacing the file and replacing the process are separate acts, and Windows cannot do the second at all, so the answer says which case this is. Refused in a container and when the check is switched off.

200.description: In place; the answer says whether a restart is needed or possible

400.description: Already current, switched off, or running in a container

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

500.description: The download or the checksum failed

post.summary: Ask the release feed now, rather than waiting out the cached answer
post.description: The version card is built from an answer the application keeps for six hours, because the release feed allows an unauthenticated caller sixty requests an hour per address and every open card would otherwise spend them. That is right for a screen refreshing itself and wrong for the minute after somebody publishes a release, when the card states a version that was newest this morning. This asks the feed at once and answers with the same body as `GET /settings/update`, so the card can be drawn again from what comes back. It has a limit of its own - once every five minutes for the whole installation - and refuses with `updateCheckedRecently` and the seconds remaining, so the button cannot hand back the problem the cache prevents. A feed that will not answer is reported as `problem` with a 200, exactly as the GET does. Needs the rights the built-in administrator has, not merely settings:manage.

201.description: The running version and what is available, freshly asked

403.description: Not an administrator of this installation

409.description: Asked too recently, or the update check is switched off

get.description: The plan, the backups kept on the server, newest first, and whether one can be made - which takes BACKUP_PASSPHRASE of at least twelve characters on the server. Needs settings:manage, because a backup is the whole installation.

post.description: Reads every table but the sessions in one moment, seals it with BACKUP_PASSPHRASE, keeps it in BACKUP_DIR and removes the oldest past the number the plan keeps. Answers with the backup kept, to be downloaded. Refused as backupNeedsPassphrase where the server has no passphrase. Recorded in the administration log.

409.description: No BACKUP_PASSPHRASE of at least twelve characters

put.description: A five-field cron expression read in the installation’s timezone - empty makes no backup on its own - and how many backups are kept. A schedule the scheduler could not read is refused rather than stored. Answers with the whole card. Recorded in the administration log.

400.description: A schedule that would never run, or a number outside 1 to 365

get.description: The sealed file, as it is kept. Recorded in the administration log, because it is a copy of the whole installation leaving the server.

Whoever holds `queues:write` reaches every queue and is shown every role's access; anybody else is shown only the queues their role reaches, with their own line of the access - a queue they do not reach is not found rather than refused.

post.description: Takes `queues:write`. Needs a `name`. `parentId` puts the queue under another for finding it; access is the queue's own and not its parent's. `access` lists `roleId` and `level` - `read` reaches the queue's tickets to read them, `write` to create and change them too - and a role with no line does not reach the queue. `followUp` is what an answer to a closed ticket does: `reopen`, the default, `reject` or `new-ticket`. `unlockMinutes` frees a ticket locked to an owner who does nothing with it, from 1 to 10080; 0, the default, never does.

get.description: Takes `tickets:read`. One page of the tickets in the queues the caller reaches, the most recently changed first, and `totalCount` saying how many there are altogether. `queue` narrows to one queue, `state` to a comma-separated list of state ids, `unfinished=true` to tickets somebody still has to do something about, `owner` to an agent's id or `me`, `contact` and `organisation` to one customer's, and `q` to a title or number holding the words. `limit` is 50 unless given and at most 200 - more is refused rather than quietly lowered - and `page` counts from 1.

400.description: A limit above 200, or a filter that is not a number

post.description: Takes `tickets:create` and a queue the caller's role works in and that still takes tickets. Needs a `title`, a `queueId` and the `body` of the article it starts from, written as a `note` or a `phone` call (`channel`, a note unless said) and shown to the customer only when `customerVisible`; `minutes` notes the time worked for it. `stateId`, `priorityId` and `typeId` default to new, normal and unclassified; a pending state needs `pendingUntil` in the future, and merged is reached by merging and never chosen. The number is the day in the installation's zone and the id. `contactId` names who the ticket is for, a contact still offered, and brings the contact's organisation along unless `organisationId` is given. `serviceLevelId` puts it under a service level other than the one its queue starts tickets with; what it is owed is counted from its opening.

409.description: The queue is only read, or something chosen is no longer offered

get.summary: Who a ticket in a queue can be given to
get.description: Takes `tickets:read` and a `queue` the caller reaches: the accounts on the staff side whose role works tickets there.

Takes `tickets:read`. With the minutes noted on it and whether the caller watches it. A ticket is reached through its queue, and one in a queue the caller's role does not reach is not found rather than refused.

put.description: Takes `tickets:write`; a field left out stays as it was, and every change is written to the ticket's history by the names things had then. Moving it takes working in the queue it goes to. `clearOwner`, `clearResponsible`, `clearContact` and `clearOrganisation` take the person or the company off, because an id sent as null cannot be told apart from one not sent. `locked` keeps it to its owner, and locking a ticket nobody owns makes the caller its owner. A pending state needs `pendingUntil` in the future unless the ticket already waits for one; leaving it drops the moment. Changing it takes the caller's role working in its queue, or `queues:write`. A ticket is reached through its queue, and one in a queue the caller's role does not reach is not found rather than refused. `serviceLevelId` puts it under another service level, counting what it is owed afresh from its opening, and `clearServiceLevel` under none.

bearerAuth.description: A personal API token. Not subject to the CSRF check, since a browser never sends this header on its own.

sessionCookie.name: gts_session
sessionCookie.description: A browser session. State-changing calls made with this must also echo the gts_csrf cookie in the X-CSRF-Token header and come from this origin; calls authenticated by a personal API token are exempt. A call carrying `X-Background-Request: 1` is held to the session's lifetime and idle timeout like any other but is not counted as the session being used - the interface sends it on the checks it makes by itself, so that a screen left open is signed out by the idle timeout. Opening the event stream counts the same way.

csrfToken.name: X-CSRF-Token
csrfToken.description: The value of the gts_csrf cookie, echoed back. Required alongside sessionCookie on POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
